stem: A 26-year-old woman with major depression says she plans to take all her prescribed tablets tonight and has written a goodbye message. She declines admission and says she will 'promise to be safe' if discharged. She has no intoxication or psychosis.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate action?
options: Accept the verbal safety promise and discharge with a routine appointment in four weeks.
Arrange urgent psychiatric assessment, continuous safe supervision and a collaborative plan for restricting access to means.
Tell her family the exact details in front of other patients without seeking consent.
Prescribe an increased antidepressant dose and discharge the same day without observation.
Document a low score on a single suicide screening tool to justify discharge.
explanations: A no-suicide promise does not reliably mitigate an imminent, specific risk with available means.
Correct: specific plan, intent indicators and access to means require immediate risk management and senior assessment.
Disclosure should be proportional to serious risk, privacy obligations and consent where feasible; public discussion is inappropriate.
Medication changes take time and do not replace immediate safety measures for active suicidal intent.
Risk tools alone do not replace an individual formulation, collateral and assessment of imminent risk.
pearl: A specific near-term plan, preparations and access to means call for urgent intervention regardless of a numerical screening score.
pivot: If only passive death wishes without intent, plans or escalating factors, a less restrictive collaborative plan may be possible after comprehensive assessment.

steps: Ensure immediate safety
Stay with the patient in a safe environment; remove accessible medications/sharps and summon senior psychiatry/emergency support.
Assess and document
Current ideation, plan, intent, preparations, access, prior attempts, substance use, psychosis, supports and protective factors; obtain collateral appropriately.
Plan disposition
Offer voluntary admission where indicated; if refusing and acute serious risk persists, assess capacity and applicable mental health law with seniors.
Communicate
Collaborative safety planning, means restriction, family/support involvement when appropriate, crisis contacts and clear follow-up.
management.safety: Do not rely on a 'contract for safety' as an alternative to clinical assessment.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 31-year-old seven days after delivery has slept only two hours nightly, is euphoric and irritable, believes her baby has a divine mission and hears a voice giving instructions about the infant. She is restless and repeatedly attempts to leave the ward with the baby.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate management?
options: Reassure her that 'baby blues' commonly include delusions and advise rest at home.
Start an SSRI alone and review at the routine six-week postnatal check.
Keep the baby with her unsupervised to preserve bonding while observing her mood.
Urgently assess mother–infant safety and arrange psychiatric admission/supervision with acute antipsychotic or mood stabilising treatment as indicated.
Offer CBT as sole treatment because symptoms started after childbirth.
explanations: Postpartum blues do not cause frank psychosis; this presentation is a psychiatric emergency.
Antidepressant monotherapy can worsen mania and is inadequate for psychosis with infant-related risk.
Safety of mother and infant is paramount; supervision and safeguarding must precede routine bonding arrangements.
Correct: postpartum psychosis needs rapid specialist inpatient care, risk assessment and appropriate pharmacological treatment.
Psychotherapy is supportive later but cannot replace emergency treatment of postpartum psychosis.
pearl: Postpartum psychosis usually emerges rapidly after childbirth, often with mood elevation or psychotic symptoms, and requires urgent safety-focused care.
pivot: Isolated tearfulness and sleep disturbance without delusions, hallucinations or risk may be baby blues or postnatal depression depending duration/severity.

steps: Protect both patients
Do not leave infant alone with acutely psychotic parent until assessed; request urgent maternal mental health and obstetric review.
Assess
Risk to self/baby, voices and commands, beliefs, sleep, bipolar history, medical causes and medication/substance exposure.
Treat
Arrange admission (mother–baby unit when appropriate and safe); supervised antipsychotic and/or mood stabilising therapy per perinatal psychiatry team, restore sleep.
Support family
Sensitive family involvement, infant care plan and breastfeeding/medication compatibility counselling.
management.safety: Never assume psychotic beliefs are harmless because the parent seems affectionate toward the baby.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 42-year-old on sertraline has recently started linezolid. After one day she develops agitation, diaphoresis, temperature 39.2 °C, diarrhoea, inducible ankle clonus and hyperreflexia. CK is modestly elevated.
ask: Which diagnosis and first approach are MOST appropriate?
options: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: continue sertraline and give haloperidol.
Anticholinergic toxicity: give physostigmine as routine initial therapy.
Septic shock: commence antibiotics and ignore the implicated interaction.
Panic attack: reassurance and discharge because the findings are functional.
Serotonin syndrome: stop serotonergic drugs, provide supportive care and benzodiazepines, escalating for hyperthermia.
explanations: NMS is usually associated with dopamine antagonists and prominent rigidity/bradyreflexia; extra serotonin blockade would be inappropriate.
Anticholinergic toxicity features dry skin and reduced bowel activity, not diaphoresis, diarrhoea and clonus.
Infection must be assessed if plausible, but characteristic clonus/hyperreflexia after serotonergic interaction demands immediate drug cessation.
High fever, autonomic instability and inducible clonus are objective toxicity signs.
Correct: serotonergic excess causes a triad of neuromuscular, autonomic and mental-state changes; removing the cause is immediate.
pearl: Clonus and hyperreflexia strongly favour serotonin syndrome over the 'lead-pipe' rigidity of NMS.
pivot: If symptoms arise days after dopamine-antagonist exposure with severe rigidity and elevated CK, consider NMS.

steps: Stop contributors
Cease serotonergic medicines and review all interacting prescriptions with pharmacy/infectious diseases.
Stabilise
ABCDE, IV fluids if needed, external cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation/tremor; check CK, electrolytes and renal function.
Escalate
Critical care for severe hyperthermia/rigidity/organ dysfunction; consider specialist-directed serotonin antagonism.
management.safety: Antipyretics are ineffective for hyperthermia from muscular activity; avoid physical restraints that increase heat generation.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 51-year-old who drinks 20 units of alcohol daily stopped drinking 24 hours ago. He is sweating, anxious and tremulous, pulse 112/min. He has a history of withdrawal seizures but no current hallucinations or severe liver disease.
options: Prescribe a supervised symptom-triggered benzodiazepine withdrawal regimen with thiamine and close monitoring.
Give haloperidol alone to prevent seizures and leave him unattended.
Give IV glucose alone before thiamine in a malnourished patient and discharge once calmer.
Give a single oral sleeping tablet and advise him to resume alcohol at home.
Wait until delirium develops because withdrawal treatment is only indicated after hallucinations.
explanations: Correct: benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal seizures; thiamine protects against Wernicke encephalopathy and monitoring detects deterioration.
Antipsychotics do not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures and can lower seizure threshold.
Hypoglycaemia must be treated immediately if present, but thiamine is important and glucose alone does not treat withdrawal.
Unsupervised alcohol resumption and inadequate sedation are not a safe management plan.
A seizure history and autonomic findings indicate high risk requiring early treatment and monitoring.
pearl: Alcohol withdrawal can progress from tremor to seizures and delirium tremens; benzodiazepines and thiamine are core treatment.
pivot: If profound confusion, visual hallucinations and autonomic instability emerge at 48–96 hours, evaluate delirium tremens with higher-acuity care.

steps: Assess
ABCDE, withdrawal severity scale, history of seizures/DT, co-ingestion, electrolytes, glucose, magnesium and hepatic function.
Prevent seizures
Supervised benzodiazepine regimen adjusted to severity and risk; thiamine before or alongside nutrition/glucose if feasible without delaying hypoglycaemia rescue.
Monitor
Frequent observations, cognition, hydration, electrolytes and sedation level; escalate for seizures, hallucinations, severe agitation or respiratory depression.
Plan recovery
After stabilisation offer addiction team, relapse prevention treatment and psychosocial supports.
management.safety: Phenobarbital or other adjuncts require local protocols and specialist supervision; never omit monitoring in high-risk withdrawal.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 79-year-old two days after hip surgery is disorientated, sees insects on the wall and alternates between drowsiness and agitation over hours. He was cognitively intact before admission. He has a urinary catheter and received opioids overnight.
ask: What is the MOST appropriate first management strategy?
options: Diagnose schizophrenia and commence a long-term antipsychotic plan.
Treat possible precipitants and provide orientation, sleep, sensory aids and safe supervision; use short-term medication only if severe distress/risk.
Administer high-dose benzodiazepines routinely as first line for all delirium.
Ignore confusion because postoperative hallucinations always resolve without complication.
Obtain a psychiatric inpatient transfer before checking vital signs or glucose.
explanations: Sudden onset with fluctuating attention following illness/surgery indicates delirium, not a chronic primary psychosis.
Correct: delirium care prioritises identifying causes, non-drug measures and cautious symptom management.
Benzodiazepines often worsen non-withdrawal delirium and carry respiratory/fall risks.
Delirium can indicate infection, drug toxicity, hypoxia or metabolic illness and predicts adverse outcomes.
Immediate medical assessment for reversible precipitants is essential.
pearl: Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention/awareness; always seek medical precipitants and medication effects.
pivot: Gradual progressive cognitive decline without fluctuation suggests dementia, although dementia also increases delirium vulnerability.

steps: Screen and stabilise
Assess ABC, oxygenation, glucose, pain, urine retention, constipation, infection and medication toxicity.
Support
Reorientation, hearing aids/glasses, family presence, day-night routine, mobility, hydration and minimisation of unnecessary catheters.
Escalate if dangerous
Supervised low-dose antipsychotic only for severe distress/behavioural risk after non-drug measures and QT/Parkinson risk review.
Document
Monitor daily for resolution and communicate cognitive baseline to carers.
management.safety: Avoid antipsychotics in Lewy body dementia or Parkinsonism unless senior specialist-directed; check QT risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 35-year-old woman attends GP repeatedly for abdominal pain. Her partner answers every question and refuses to leave. When seen briefly alone she reveals he controls her money and has threatened to hurt her if she leaves. She asks that no details be disclosed to him.
ask: What is the BEST initial response?
options: Call the partner into the room to confront him and explain why threats are unacceptable.
Arrange a private, trauma-informed safety assessment, document objectively and discuss safe referral and disclosure limits.
Tell her she must leave the relationship today and contact police without discussing her preferences.
Promise absolute confidentiality even if there is imminent danger to a child or another person.
Treat pain only and avoid discussing the threats because this is a non-medical issue.
explanations: Confrontation can increase immediate danger, especially with coercive control.
Correct: respect autonomy, confidentiality and immediate safety while offering specialist supports.
A blanket directive can increase risk; mandatory reporting/legal duties depend on local law and specific risks.
Confidentiality has legally defined limits in serious safety situations; explain these honestly.
Family violence has direct medical and safety consequences and deserves compassionate clinical response.
pearl: Coercive control is a serious form of abuse; ask privately, check immediate danger and avoid actions that may increase retaliation.
pivot: If a child is at risk or imminent serious harm exists, statutory safeguarding duties may justify limited disclosures under local law.

steps: Create privacy
See the patient without partner; ask whether it is safe to talk and which communication channels are safe.
Assess safety
Immediate threats, weapons, strangulation, escalation, children/dependents and safe place to go; seek emergency help if imminent danger.
Plan collaboratively
Validate disclosure without judgement, offer domestic-violence service contacts, safe documentation and follow-up.
Safeguard information
Explain confidentiality and statutory disclosure obligations; avoid printing unsafe messages or sending alerts to shared devices.
management.safety: Never assume that 'just leave' is a safe intervention; departure can be a period of increased risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: An 80-year-old taking apixaban for AF presents with melaena, BP 86/48 mmHg, Hb 69 g/L and ongoing haematemesis. Last apixaban dose was five hours ago. He is confused and cool peripherally.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate immediate plan?
options: Continue apixaban to prevent stroke and arrange routine endoscopy in a week.
Give oral vitamin K because it rapidly reverses all direct oral anticoagulants.
Arrange discharge on oral iron once the blood pressure transiently improves.
Hold apixaban, resuscitate/transfuse as needed and urgently discuss specific reversal plus endoscopic source control.
Start therapeutic IV heparin as a bridge while awaiting endoscopy.
explanations: Life-threatening active bleeding requires interrupting anticoagulation and emergency haemostasis.
Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not factor Xa inhibitors such as apixaban.
Severe GI haemorrhage and shock require inpatient resuscitation and definitive care.
Correct: major DOAC-associated bleeding warrants haemodynamic resuscitation and targeted reversal consideration.
Additional anticoagulation increases active bleeding and is unsafe.
pearl: In major DOAC bleeding, stop the drug, stabilise physiology, consider reversal for life-threatening haemorrhage and control the source.
pivot: For minor self-limited bleeding, temporary interruption without reversal may be sufficient depending on risk and timing.

steps: Resuscitate
ABCDE, IV access, crossmatch, blood products guided by physiology and bleeding, group and urgent gastro/endoscopy consultation.
Reverse appropriately
Stop apixaban; senior haematology review for factor Xa inhibitor reversal (specific agent or PCC based on availability/indication).
Find source
Urgent therapeutic endoscopy when stabilised; PPI if suspected ulcer and other source-specific treatment.
After haemostasis
Reassess thromboembolism risk and timing of resuming anticoagulation with specialists.
management.safety: Do not use vitamin K or protamine as routine apixaban reversal; document time of last dose and renal function.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 43-year-old with obesity presents with tiredness and thirst. HbA1c is 82 mmol/mol (9.7%) and fasting glucose 13 mmol/L. He is not acidotic, has no ketones or catabolic weight loss, and renal function is normal.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate initial management?
options: Explain the diagnosis, assess complications/cardiovascular risk, start lifestyle support and pharmacotherapy with early reassessment.
Recommend six months of dietary change only and avoid medication until HbA1c exceeds 11%.
Diagnose type 1 diabetes automatically because he reports thirst and fatigue.
Discharge without follow-up if the urine ketone test is negative.
Commence IV insulin infusion and admit everyone with HbA1c above 80 mmol/mol.
explanations: Correct: significant hyperglycaemia needs a structured treatment plan, not lifestyle advice alone; drug choice is individualised.
Marked symptomatic hyperglycaemia deserves timely pharmacological intervention and close follow-up.
Symptoms alone do not distinguish diabetes subtype; evaluate phenotype, ketones and autoimmune features when clinically indicated.
Absence of DKA does not remove long-term organ and vascular risk requiring treatment.
IV insulin is for metabolic emergencies or selected severe inpatient situations, not all stable type 2 diabetes.
pearl: New type 2 diabetes management includes lifestyle, individualised glucose-lowering drugs, cardiovascular/renal risk and retinal/foot screening.
pivot: Marked ketosis, rapid weight loss, dehydration or acidosis raises concern for insulin deficiency/DKA and changes urgency.

steps: Assess
Confirm glucose pattern, symptoms and ketones; renal function, BP, lipids, urine ACR, eye/foot screening and cardiovascular risk.
Treat
Diet/activity support and pharmacotherapy, commonly metformin if suitable; consider early combination or insulin for very high symptomatic glucose, guided by comorbidities.
Review soon
Home glucose review, adherence, education and hypoglycaemia safety when applicable; titrate treatment within weeks.
Protect organs
Discuss smoking cessation, vaccinations, BP/lipids and kidney/cardiovascular protective agents when indicated.
management.safety: Do not start metformin in significant metabolic acidosis or unstable renal failure; selection depends on eGFR and risk.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 59-year-old at day nine after chemotherapy for lymphoma has temperature 38.7 °C, rigors and ANC 0.2 × 10^9/L. BP 103/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 96%. He has a central venous catheter and no focal symptoms.
options: Give oral amoxicillin and discharge once temperature falls.
Wait for an absolute neutrophil count tomorrow because today's value may be transient.
Obtain blood cultures promptly and give empiric antipseudomonal IV antibiotics without significant delay.
Give granulocyte colony-stimulating factor as sole acute infection treatment.
Withhold antibiotics until a pathogen is grown from the central line.
explanations: High-risk febrile neutropenia requires urgent inpatient broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and monitoring.
Sepsis can progress rapidly in neutropenia; treatment must not wait for repeat results.
Correct: febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency even without shock or a clear source.
G-CSF may be considered in selected cases but does not replace empiric antibiotics.
Microbiological confirmation often takes days; early treatment is lifesaving.
pearl: Fever after chemotherapy with profound neutropenia is presumptive infection until proven otherwise; normal blood pressure does not justify delay.
pivot: A stable low-risk neutropenic patient may be considered for selected oral/outpatient pathways after structured risk assessment and specialist input.

steps: Recognise and refer
Sepsis assessment, IV access, neutropenic precautions and urgent oncology/haematology review.
Sample
Blood cultures from peripheral and each central line lumen as appropriate, FBC, renal/liver function, lactate and focused source tests.
Treat
Begin IV broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotic promptly per hospital neutropenic fever protocol; add coverage based on instability/resistance.
Monitor
Frequent vital signs, culture adjustment, review for invasive fungal disease if fever persists, haemodynamic escalation when needed.
management.safety: Avoid routine rectal examination and delaying antibiotics for imaging.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.

stem: A 67-year-old on dialysis says he wishes to stop treatment because its burdens outweigh the benefits. He calmly explains that death may occur sooner, can describe alternatives and consequences, and maintains the decision over several discussions. No delirium or severe depression is evident.
ask: Which is the MOST appropriate response?
options: Continue dialysis against his will because stopping treatment could cause death.
Accept the informed refusal after confirming decision-specific capacity, discuss symptom-focused care and document the conversation.
Ask family to override the patient's preference because the decision is emotionally difficult.
Assess capacity by MMSE score alone and treat any score below 30 as incapacity.
Record 'suicidal intent' automatically and refer for compulsory psychiatric treatment.
explanations: A capable adult can refuse burdensome life-sustaining treatment even when clinicians disagree.
Correct: capacity concerns understanding, appreciation, weighing and communication; autonomy coexists with a duty to offer palliative support.
Family opinions matter if invited and for substitutes if incapacity exists, but do not automatically override capable refusal.
Capacity is specific to the decision/time; MMSE is not a legal substitute for structured capacity assessment.
Informed refusal of treatment is not automatically suicidality; assess depression and coercion without assuming incapacity.
pearl: Respect informed refusal when a patient has decision-specific capacity; support symptom management and advance-care planning.
pivot: If fluctuating delirium impairs understanding/appreciation, treat reversible causes and consider the applicable substitute-decision process.

steps: Assess capacity
Explain prognosis, dialysis alternatives and consequences in understandable language; elicit teach-back and consistent reasoning.
Explore values
Ask about burdens, symptoms, coercion, supports and treatable depression/delirium; involve family with consent.
Plan safely
Document the decision, contact nephrology and palliative care, and establish symptom control and emergency plans.
Review
Offer opportunities to revisit preferences without coercion; follow local legal and advance-care-directive processes.
management.safety: A patient may make a decision clinicians believe unwise while still having capacity.
management.local: Educational pathway: follow local mental health, prescribing, capacity and safeguarding policies and seek immediate senior help where indicated.
